title: Single Link Removal Perturbation in Szegedy Quantum Walk: from Graph Completeness Testing to Integrity Monitoring
abstract: We present a rigorous perturbative analysis of the Szegedy quantum walk search algorithm on the complete graph with marked nodes, when a specific anomaly is present in the graph. This is motivated by the problem of monitoring the integrity of dense trusted communication networks with a quantum-assisted procedure. The topology of these networks is modeled as a complete graph, and the anomaly of interest is the disappearance of a single communication link which represents the minimal and spectrally hardest structural defect to detect. Building on the graph-completeness testing algorithm framework, we quantify how the removal of a single unmarked-unmarked edge propagates through the relevant spectral quantities of the Szegedy quantum walk. Denoting by $n$ the total number of nodes of the graph and by $m$ the number of marked nodes, we prove that the perturbation to the transition matrix has spectral norm $Θ(1/n)$, and that the gap eigenvalue undergoes a strictly negative first-order shift for every $n$ and every number of marked nodes $m$, providing a formal proof of a conjecture from our completeness testing algorithm work; in the regime $m = Θ(n)$ relevant for the search algorithm, this shift has magnitude $Θ(1/n^2)$. The corresponding eigenphase shift satisfies $Δθ_\star = Θ(1/n^2)$ in the same regime. We establish that the rotation angle of the effective subspace under this perturbation is $O(1/n)$ for $m = Θ(n)$. Finally, we bound the change in success probability to $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ in this same regime of marked nodes, and show that this bound is dominated by the geometric misalignment of the effective subspace rather than by the spectral shift of the eigenphase. These results provide both the theoretical foundations and the fundamental scaling limits of quantum walk-based topology integrity monitoring under minimal structural perturbations.
summary: This paper provides a deep theoretical analysis of detecting single link failures in dense quantum networks modeled by the Szegedy quantum walk. By applying perturbation theory, the authors derive precise scaling laws showing how the loss of one edge causes measurable shifts in spectral quantities like eigenvalues and phases. These results establish fundamental limits for quantum-assisted topology integrity monitoring.
main_problem: The paper develops a rigorous perturbative analysis to detect structural anomalies, specifically the removal of a single link, in dense quantum communication networks.
main_result: It quantifies that this minimal perturbation causes predictable, small shifts ($\Theta(1/n^2)$) in spectral quantities like the gap eigenvalue and eigenphase shift, allowing for detection with high theoretical precision.
method: The analysis employs time-dependent perturbation theory applied to the Szegedy quantum walk operator, analyzing how low-rank modifications affect the spectrum of the system's discriminant matrix.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum walk executed on a complete graph ($K_n$) representing a dense communication network. The process uses the Szegedy quantum walk algorithm framework to test for link integrity.
key_observables: Spectral norm of the perturbation ($\Theta(1/n)$), shift in the gap eigenvalue ($\Theta(1/n^2)$), eigenphase shift ($\Delta	heta^\star = \Theta(1/n^2)$), and change in success probability ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$).
important_parameters: The analysis is most relevant in the regime where the number of marked nodes $m$ scales linearly with the total number of nodes, i.e., $m = \Theta(n)$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the anomaly is the removal of a single unmarked-unmarked edge, and the analysis relies on first-order perturbation theory for eigenvalue shifts.
paper_structure: The paper builds from graph completeness testing to integrity monitoring. It analyzes the spectral consequences of removing an edge $\{u, v\} \subseteq V \setminus M$ by treating it as a small perturbation ($\Delta$) on the transition matrix $P$, leading to detailed calculations of eigenvalue shifts and success probability bounds.
why_interesting: The rigorous quantification of detection limits based on spectral perturbations is highly relevant for understanding noise resilience in quantum communication protocols and network security.
